Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

while conjunction

during the time that

also whilst, as (while), during the time that

classical

Sen. Ep. 7.8: hominēs, dum docent, discunt
Hor. S. 1.5.71–72: paene … ārsit dum turdōs versat in ignī

dum (+ present indicative)

conjunction, with the present indicative, even of past time

The longer action during which something else happens. Latin keeps the present after dum even when the main verb is past: ārsit dum … versat, he caught fire while he was turning. Where the two last equally long, “as long as”, see that record.

Other words

  • cum (+ imperfect subjunctive) — while, as (in past narrative)

    conjunction, with the imperfect subjunctive · also used · classical · Cic. Tusc. 5.97: Sōcratēn ferunt, cum ūsque ad vesperum contentius ambulāret …

    The background against which a past event happens.

  • participium praesentis — while (doing)

    the present participle, agreeing with its noun · also used · classical · Cic. Sen. 17: ille autem clāvum tenēns quiētus sedeat in puppī

    “While holding”, “while walking”: the commonest Latin for an English “while …ing”. Lewis & Short has participium as the grammarians’ word (Varro, Quintilian).

Examples

  • mūtuō ista fīunt, et hominēs, dum docent, discunt

    it works both ways: people learn while they teachSen. Ep. 7.8

  • diēs nihil est. dum versās tē, nox fit

    a day is nothing. While you turn round, night fallsPetr. 41.4

  • sēdulus hospes paene macrōs ārsit dum turdōs versat in ignī

    our busy host nearly caught fire while he was turning the lean thrushes on the fireHor. S. 1.5.71–72

  • dum differtur vīta trānscurrit

    while it is put off, life runs pastSen. Ep. 1.2

  • Sōcratēn ferunt, cum ūsque ad vesperum contentius ambulāret quaesītumque esset ex eō quārē id faceret, respondisse sē, quō melius cēnāret, obsōnāre ambulandō famem

    they say that Socrates, when he was walking hard till evening and was asked why, answered that he was buying in hunger by walking, so as to dine betterCic. Tusc. 5.97

See also as long as, whereas, when.
